title: Quantifying Mixed-state Entanglement Via Partial Transpose And Realignment Moments
authors: Poetri Sonya Tarabunga And Tobias Haug
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2194 (2026).

Entanglement plays a crucial role in quantum information science and many-body physics, yet quantifying it in mixed quantum many-body systems has remained a notoriously difficult problem. Here, we introduce families of quantitative entanglement witnesses, constructed from partial transpose and realignment moments, which provide rigorous bounds on entanglement monotones as well as entanglement dimensionality. Our witnesses can be efficiently measured using SWAP tests or variants of Bell measurements, thus making them directly implementable on current hardware. Leveraging our witnesses, we present several novel results on entanglement properties of mixed states, both in quantum information and many-body physics. We develop efficient algorithms to test whether mixed states with bounded entropy have low or high entanglement, which previously was only possible for pure states. We also provide an efficient algorithm to test the Schmidt rank using only two-copy measurements, and the operator Schmidt rank using four-copy measurements. Further, our witnesses robustly certify the quantum circuit depth in the presence of noise, as well as the Schmidt rank of mixed states. Finally, we show that the entanglement phase diagram of Haar random states, quantified by the partial transpose negativity, can be fully established solely by computing our witness, a result that also applies to any state [MATH]-design. Our witnesses can also be efficiently computed for matrix product states, thus enabling the characterization of entanglement in extensive many-body systems. Finally, we make progress on the entanglement required for quantum cryptography, establishing rigorous limits on pseudoentanglement and pseudorandom density matrices with bounded entropy. Our work opens new avenues for quantifying entanglement in large and noisy quantum systems.

.
tldr: The paper introduces families of entanglement witnesses based on partial transpose and realignment moments that provide rigorous bounds on mixed-state entanglement monotones and dimensionality, with efficient measurement protocols and applications to many-body and cryptographic settings.
motivation: Quantifying entanglement in mixed quantum many-body systems is notoriously difficult, especially for large and noisy states where existing methods are limited or inefficient.
method: The authors construct quantitative entanglement witnesses from partial transpose and realignment moments, measurable via SWAP tests or Bell measurement variants, and develop efficient algorithms for testing entanglement and Schmidt rank using two- and four-copy measurements.
result: The witnesses yield rigorous bounds on entanglement monotones and dimensionality, certify circuit depth under noise, characterize entanglement phase diagrams for Haar random states, and establish limits on pseudoentanglement and pseudorandom density matrices.
conclusion: This work provides a practical and scalable framework for quantifying entanglement in mixed states, with direct implementability on current hardware and broad implications for quantum information and many-body physics.

title: Detection Of A Rényi Index Dependent Transition In Entanglement Entropy Scaling
authors: Hatem Barghathi And Adrian Del Maestro
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2184 (2026).

The scaling of entanglement with subsystem size encodes key information about phases and criticality, but the von Neumann entropy is costly to access in experiments and simulations, often requiring full state tomography. The second Rényi entropy is readily measured using two-copy protocols and is often used as a proxy for the von Neumann entanglement entropy, where it is assumed to track its asymptotic scaling. Sugino and Korepiny (Int. J. Mod. Phys. B 32, 1850306 (2018)) revealed that in the ground state of some highly constrained spin models, the scaling of the von Neumann and Rényi entropies can differ, varying from power law to logarithmic scaling as a function of the Rényi index. Here, we construct a number-conserving many-body state that demonstrates a Rényi-index-dependent change in the leading entanglement scaling, generalizing previous results to the case of interacting fermions. We introduce a symmetry-aware lower bound on the von Neumann entropy built from charge-resolved Rényi entropies that can provide a protocol for diagnosing anomalous entanglement scaling from experimentally accessible data.

.
tldr: Constructs a number-conserving many-body state that exhibits a Rényi-index-dependent transition in entanglement entropy scaling, and introduces a symmetry-aware lower bound on von Neumann entropy from charge-resolved Rényi entropies.
motivation: The von Neumann entropy is costly to access, while the second Rényi entropy is experimentally friendly and often used as a proxy, but their asymptotic scaling can differ in constrained spin models. This work generalizes such anomalous scaling to interacting fermions and provides an experimentally accessible diagnostic.
method: The authors construct a number-conserving many-body state and analyze the scaling of Rényi and von Neumann entropies as a function of the Rényi index, then derive a symmetry-aware lower bound on the von Neumann entropy from charge-resolved Rényi entropies.
result: They demonstrate a Rényi-index-dependent change in the leading entanglement scaling, varying from power law to logarithmic, generalizing previous results to interacting fermions. The lower bound offers a protocol for diagnosing anomalous entanglement scaling from experimentally accessible data.
conclusion: Rényi entropies can exhibit qualitatively different scaling than the von Neumann entropy, and charge-resolved Rényi entropies can bound the von Neumann entropy, enabling experimental detection of anomalous entanglement scaling.

title: Quantifiers And Witnesses For The Nonclassicality Of Measurements And Of States
authors: Yujie Zhang, Yìlè Yīng, And David Schmid
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2180 (2026).

In recent work [Phys. Rev. X 16, 021050], we proposed a unified notion of nonclassicality that applies to arbitrary processes in quantum theory, including individual quantum states, measurements, and sets thereof. This notion is derived from the principle of generalized noncontextuality, but in a novel manner that applies to individual processes rather than full experiments or theories. In the present work, we develop semidefinite-programming-based certificates and witnesses for the nonclassicality of states, sources, measurements, and sets thereof. These theory-dependent methods complement theory-independent approaches based on noncontextuality inequalities. We demonstrate the framework through a variety of explicit examples.

.
tldr: Develops semidefinite-programming-based quantifiers and witnesses for the nonclassicality of quantum states, measurements, and sets thereof.
motivation: To provide practical certificates for a recently proposed unified notion of nonclassicality based on generalized noncontextuality, complementing theory-independent noncontextuality inequalities.
method: Formulates semidefinite-programming-based certificates and witnesses that are theory-dependent and apply to individual quantum processes, including states, sources, and measurements.
result: Demonstrates the framework through explicit examples, yielding quantifiers and witnesses that can detect and quantify nonclassicality in various scenarios.
conclusion: The methods offer a versatile toolbox for characterizing nonclassicality in arbitrary quantum processes, bridging foundational concepts with computational certifications.

title: Violation Of Bell Inequalities In 2 × 3 ...
authors: Paweł Caban And Paweł Horodecki
abstract: We consider the Clauser–Horne (CH) inequality for a qubit–qutrit system. We derive the necessary and sufficient conditions for the violation of the inequality as well as some simple sufficient conditions. Remarkably, we demonstrate the importance of local parameters in violation of the inequality. In other words, there are some families of mixed states violating the inequality for which the correlation part alone is useless in the CH test.
tldr: Derives necessary and sufficient conditions for violating the Clauser-Horne inequality in a qubit-qutrit system, revealing that local parameters can be essential for violation.
motivation: Bell inequality violations are central to quantum nonlocality and device-independent protocols, yet conditions for mixed states in higher dimensions remain less understood.
method: Analyzes the CH inequality for 2×3 systems, separating correlation and local parameter contributions to derive violation conditions.
result: Obtains necessary and sufficient conditions for violation plus simple sufficient conditions, and shows families of mixed states where correlation alone is useless but local parameters enable CH violation.
conclusion: Highlights the nontrivial role of local parameters in Bell tests, with implications for characterizing nonlocality in mixed-dimensional systems.

title: Streaming Belief Propagation On Mixed-Alphabet Tanner Graphs For Practical Quantum Memory
authors: Kao-Yueh Kuo And Ching-Yi Lai
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2207 (2026).

Reliable quantum memory under circuit-level noise requires decoders that can process syndrome information continuously and at a rate comparable to its generation. In practical quantum error correction (QEC), repeated syndrome measurements cause the number of potential error locations to grow rapidly with both code size and time. In this paper, we propose a streaming mixed-alphabet belief propagation (SM-BP) decoder. We construct a space-time Tanner graph across multiple rounds of syndrome extraction with mixed-alphabet error variables, preserving correlations arising from multi-qubit faults. Additionally, we propose an adaptive sliding window procedure that captures long error events across window boundaries and adjusts the decoding in real time. To enhance SM-BP, we introduce a technique of probabilistic error consolidation to mitigate degeneracy effects and short cycles. Our simulations demonstrate high error thresholds of 0.4% to 0.87% and strong error-floor performance for topological code families, including rotated toric, toric color, and twisted XZZX toric codes. These results show that SM-BP provides a practical decoding framework for continuous QEC under circuit-level noise.

.
tldr: The paper proposes a streaming mixed-alphabet belief propagation decoder for quantum memory that continuously processes circuit-level syndrome data using a space-time Tanner graph and adaptive sliding window.
motivation: Reliable quantum memory under circuit-level noise requires decoders that can handle rapidly growing syndrome information in real time as code size and time increase.
method: It constructs a space-time Tanner graph with mixed-alphabet error variables to preserve multi-qubit fault correlations, uses an adaptive sliding window to capture long error events, and applies probabilistic error consolidation to mitigate degeneracy and short cycles.
result: Simulations demonstrate high error thresholds of 0.4% to 0.87% and strong error-floor performance for rotated toric, toric color, and twisted XZZX toric code families.
conclusion: The proposed SM-BP decoder provides a practical framework for continuous quantum error correction under circuit-level noise.

title: Simple Logical Quantum Computation With Concatenated Symplectic Double Codes
authors: Noah Berthusen And Elijah Durso-Sabina
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2195 (2026).

There have been significant recent advances in constructing theoretical and practical quantum error correcting codes that function well as quantum memories; however, performing fault-tolerant logical gates on these codes is less studied, and the protocols that do exist often require significant complexity. Building off the symplectic double construction, we investigate concatenated symplectic double codes, which have a rich set of logical gates implementable using only physical single-qubit gates and qubit relabeling. Combined with injected fold-transversal gates, the full Clifford group on a single codeblock is achieved through a functionally simple circuit. We perform circuit-level simulations of state preparation and quantum error correction on these codes and show that they have promising performance at near state-of-the-art physical error rates. As such, we argue that concatenated symplectic double codes are strong contenders as the underlying computational code on medium- to large-scale quantum computers.

.
tldr: The paper investigates concatenated symplectic double codes for simple fault-tolerant logical computation, achieving the full Clifford group with low-complexity circuits and promising circuit-level performance.
motivation: Recent advances in quantum error correcting codes have focused on memory performance, while protocols for fault-tolerant logical gates remain less studied and often complex. This work aims to find codes that support simple, experimentally feasible logical operations.
method: The authors construct concatenated symplectic double codes and analyze their logical gates, which can be implemented using only physical single-qubit gates and qubit relabeling, supplemented by injected fold-transversal gates. They perform circuit-level simulations of state preparation and quantum error correction.
result: The concatenated symplectic double codes achieve the full Clifford group on a single codeblock with a functionally simple circuit and show promising performance at near state-of-the-art physical error rates.
conclusion: These codes are strong contenders as the underlying computational code for medium- to large-scale quantum computers, offering a practical route to fault-tolerant logical gates.

title: Entanglement Growth In The Dark Intervals Of A Locally Monitored Free-fermion Chain
authors: Giovanni Di Fresco, Youenn Le Gal, Davide Valenti, Marco Schiró, And Angelo Carollo
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2183 (2026).

We consider a free fermionic chain with monitoring of the particle density on a single site of the chain and study the entanglement dynamics of quantum jump trajectories. We show that the entanglement entropy grows in time towards a stationary state which display volume law scaling of the entropy, in stark contrast with both the unitary dynamics after a local quench and the no-click limit corresponding to full post-selection. We explain the extensive entanglement growth as a consequence of the peculiar distribution of quantum jumps in time, which display superpoissonian waiting time distribution characterised by a bunching of quantum jumps followed by long dark intervals where no-clicks are detected, akin to the distribution of fluorescence light in a driven atom. We show that the presence of dark intervals is the key feature to explain the effect and that by increasing the number of sites which are monitored the volume law scaling gives away to the Zeno effect and its associated area law.

.
tldr: Monitoring a single site in a free-fermion chain leads to volume-law entanglement growth driven by clustered quantum jumps and long dark intervals.
motivation: To understand how local monitoring affects entanglement dynamics in many-body open quantum systems, contrasting unitary quench dynamics and the no-click post-selected limit.
method: Simulates quantum jump trajectories of a free fermionic chain with particle-density monitoring on one site, analyzing entanglement entropy scaling and waiting-time distributions.
result: Entanglement entropy grows to a volume-law stationary state; quantum jumps show super-Poissonian bunching with long dark intervals, and increasing monitored sites induces a Zeno effect and area-law scaling.
conclusion: Dark intervals are the key feature explaining extensive entanglement growth, revealing a monitoring-induced transition between volume-law and area-law entanglement.

title: Stabilizer Ranks, Barnes Wall Lattices And Magic Monotones
authors: Amolak Ratan Kalra And Pulkit Sinha
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2179 (2026).

In 2024, Kliuchnikov and Schönnenbeck showed a connection between the Barnes Wall lattices, stabilizer states and Clifford operations. In this work, we study their results and relate them to the problem of lower bounding stabilizer ranks. We show the first quantitative lower bound on stabilizer fidelity as a function of stabilizer ranks, which reproduces the linear-by-log lower bound for [MATH], i.e, on the approximate stabilizer rank of [MATH]. In fact, we show that the lower bound holds even when the fidelity between the approximation and [MATH] is exponentially small, which is currently the best lower bound in this regime. Next, we define a new magic monotone for pure states, the Barnes Wall norm, and its corresponding approximate variant. We upper bound these monotones by the [MATH]-count of state preparation, and also by the stabilizer ranks. In particular, the upper bound given by the [MATH]-count is tight, in the sense that we exhibit states that achieve the bound. Apart from these results, we give a Fidelity Amplification algorithm, which provides a trade-off between approximation error and the stabilizer rank. As a corollary, it gives us a way to compose approximate stabilizer decompositions into approximate decompositions of their tensor products. Finally, we provide an alternate, elementary proof of the existence and density of product states with maximal stabilizer ranks, which was first proven by Lovitz and Steffan (2022), where they used results from algebraic geometry.

.
tldr: This paper connects Barnes-Wall lattices to stabilizer ranks and magic monotones, proving new lower bounds on stabilizer fidelity and defining a Barnes-Wall norm magic monotone.
motivation: Stabilizer rank and magic monotones are central resource-theoretic tools for quantifying non-stabilizerness in fault-tolerant quantum computation, but lower bounds on stabilizer rank remain challenging and few operational monotones are known.
method: The authors build on the 2024 connection between Barnes-Wall lattices, stabilizer states, and Clifford operations to derive quantitative lower bounds on stabilizer fidelity, define the Barnes-Wall norm and its approximate variant, and introduce a fidelity amplification algorithm.
result: They obtain the first quantitative lower bound on stabilizer fidelity as a function of stabilizer rank, valid even for exponentially small fidelity, and show the Barnes-Wall norm is upper bounded by T-count and stabilizer rank, with tight instances; fidelity amplification enables composing approximate stabilizer decompositions.
conclusion: The work advances the resource theory of magic by linking lattice geometry to stabilizer-rank lower bounds and providing new monotones and composition tools relevant to magic-state quantum computation.

title: Non-secular Polariton Leakage And Dark-state Protection In Hybrid Plasmonic Cavities
authors: Marco Vallone
abstract: A major issue in exploiting plasmonic cavities as key components in nanotechnology is the effect of radiative and absorption losses on their electrodynamic behavior. Treating them as open systems, we derive a time-local, completely positive master equation that retains non-secular interference between decay pathways and reduces to the standard secular description when the environment resolves polariton splitting. When it does not, the theory predicts order-one deviations from secular leakage dynamics, including bath-induced coherences and formation of a comparatively long-lived dark polaritonic component, and provides a simple design criterion based on the ratio of polariton splitting to reservoir linewidth. A time-resolved leakage measurement, such as transmission, reflectivity, or photoluminescence, can be used to observe these effects.
tldr: Derives a time-local completely positive master equation for hybrid plasmonic cavities that captures non-secular polariton decay and predicts dark-state protection.
motivation: Plasmonic cavities suffer radiative and absorption losses, and standard secular approximations may fail when polariton splitting is comparable to reservoir linewidth.
method: Treats the cavity as an open system and derives a non-secular master equation retaining interference between decay pathways, reducing to the standard secular description when the environment resolves polariton splitting.
result: Predicts order-one deviations from secular leakage dynamics, bath-induced coherences, and a comparatively long-lived dark polaritonic component, with a design criterion based on the ratio of polariton splitting to reservoir linewidth.
conclusion: Time-resolved leakage measurements such as transmission, reflectivity, or photoluminescence can observe these effects, offering guidance for designing loss-resilient hybrid plasmonic cavities.

title: Breaking The Orthogonality Barrier In Quantum Ldpc Codes
authors: Kenta Kasai
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2205 (2026).

Classical low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes are a widely deployed and well-established technology, forming the backbone of modern communication and storage systems. It is well known that, in this classical setting, increasing the girth of the Tanner graph while maintaining regular degree distributions leads simultaneously to good belief-propagation (BP) decoding performance and large minimum distance. In the quantum setting, however, this principle does not directly apply because quantum LDPC codes must satisfy additional orthogonality constraints between their parity-check matrices. When one enforces both orthogonality and regularity in a straightforward manner, the girth is typically reduced and the minimum distance becomes structurally upper bounded. In this work, we overcome this limitation by using permutation matrices with controlled commutativity and by restricting the orthogonality constraints to only the active part of the construction, while preserving regular check-matrix structures. This design circumvents conventional structural distance limitations induced by parent-matrix orthogonality, and enables the construction of quantum LDPC codes with large girth while avoiding latent low-weight logical operators. As a concrete demonstration, we construct a girth-8, (3,12)-regular [MATH] quantum LDPC code and show that, under BP decoding combined with a low-complexity post-processing algorithm, it achieves a frame error rate as low as [MATH] on the depolarizing channel with error probability [MATH].

.
tldr: Constructs quantum LDPC codes that overcome orthogonality constraints to achieve large girth and good belief-propagation decoding performance.
motivation: Classical LDPC codes benefit from large girth and regular degree distributions, but quantum LDPC codes must satisfy orthogonality constraints that typically reduce girth and structurally limit minimum distance.
method: Uses permutation matrices with controlled commutativity and restricts orthogonality constraints to only the active part of the construction while preserving regular check-matrix structures.
result: Constructs a girth-8, (3,12)-regular quantum LDPC code that achieves a frame error rate as low as ... on the depolarizing channel with error probability ... under belief-propagation decoding with low-complexity post-processing.
conclusion: The design circumvents conventional structural distance limitations induced by parent-matrix orthogonality, enabling quantum LDPC codes with large girth and avoiding latent low-weight logical operators.

title: Floquetifying Stabiliser Codes With Distance-preserving Rewrites
authors: Benjamin Rodatz, Boldizsár Poór, And Aleks Kissinger
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2202 (2026).

Stabiliser codes with large weight measurements can be challenging to implement fault-tolerantly. To overcome this, we propose a Floquetification procedure which, given a stabiliser code, synthesises a novel Floquet code that only uses single- and two-qubit operations. Moreover, this procedure preserves the distance and number of logicals of the original code. The new Floquet code requires additional physical qubits. This overhead is linear in the weight of the largest measurement of the original code. Our method is based on the ZX calculus, a graphical language for representing and rewriting quantum circuits. However, a problem arises with the use of ZX in the context of rewriting error-correcting codes: ZX rewrites generally do not preserve code distance. Tackling this issue, we define the notion of distance-preserving rewrite that enables the transformation of error-correcting codes without changing their distance. These distance-preserving rewrites are used to decompose arbitrary weight stabiliser measurements into quantum circuits with single- and two-qubit operations. As we only use distance-preserving rewrites, we are guaranteed that a single error in the resulting circuit creates at most a single error on the data qubits. These decompositions enable us to generalise the Floquetification procedure of Townsend-Teague et al [83] to arbitrary stabiliser codes, provably preserving the distance and number of logicals of the original code.

.
tldr: The paper introduces a Floquetification procedure that converts arbitrary stabiliser codes into Floquet codes using only single- and two-qubit operations while preserving code distance and the number of logical qubits, based on distance-preserving ZX-calculus rewrites.
motivation: High-weight stabiliser measurements are challenging to implement fault-tolerantly, and existing Floquetification methods were limited to specific codes such as colour codes.
method: The authors define distance-preserving rewrites in the ZX calculus and use them to decompose arbitrary-weight stabiliser measurements into circuits with only single- and two-qubit operations.
result: The resulting Floquet code requires additional physical qubits with overhead linear in the weight of the original code's largest measurement, while provably preserving both the distance and number of logicals.
conclusion: This generalises Floquetification to arbitrary stabiliser codes, providing a systematic way to obtain fault-tolerant Floquet codes from high-weight stabiliser codes without losing error-correcting power.

title: Measurement Incompatibility In Bayesian Multiparameter Quantum Estimation
authors: Francesco Albarelli, Dominic Branford, And Jesús Rubio
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2192 (2026).

We present a comprehensive and pedagogical formulation of Bayesian multiparameter quantum estimation. Within this framework, we analyse the role of measurement incompatibility and establish its quantitative effect on attainable precision. We achieve this by deriving upper bounds based on the pretty good measurement – a notion from hypothesis testing – combined with the evaluation of the Nagaoka-Hayashi lower bound. In general, we prove that, as in the many-copy regime of local estimation theory, incompatibility can at most double the minimum loss relative to the idealised scenario in which individually optimal measurements are assumed jointly implementable. Therefore, in practical situations, the latter may provide a sufficient and computationally efficient benchmark without solving the full optimisation problem. Our results, which we illustrate through applications of discrete phase imaging, phase and dephasing estimation, and qubit sensing, provide analytical and numerical tools for assessing ultimate precision limits and the role of measurement incompatibility in Bayesian multiparameter quantum metrology, including an open-source package for all the bounds discussed here.

.
tldr: This paper presents a pedagogical Bayesian framework for multiparameter quantum estimation and shows that measurement incompatibility can at most double the minimum precision loss relative to jointly implementable optimal measurements.
motivation: Multiparameter quantum estimation is fundamentally limited by measurement incompatibility, but its quantitative effect on Bayesian precision bounds remains insufficiently understood.
method: The authors derive upper bounds based on the pretty good measurement and evaluate the Nagaoka-Hayashi lower bound, applying the results to discrete phase imaging, phase and dephasing estimation, and qubit sensing.
result: They prove that incompatibility can at most double the minimum loss compared to the idealized scenario of jointly implementable individually optimal measurements, yielding a computationally efficient benchmark.
conclusion: The work provides analytical and numerical tools, including an open-source package, for assessing ultimate precision limits and the role of measurement incompatibility in Bayesian multiparameter quantum metrology.

title: Catalytic $z$-rotations In Constant $T$-depth
authors: Isaac H. Kim
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2191 (2026).

We show that the [MATH]-depth of any single-qubit [MATH]-rotation can be reduced to [MATH] if a certain catalyst state is available. To achieve an [MATH]-approximation, it suffices to have a catalyst state of size polynomial in [MATH]. This implies that [MATH] admits a finite universal gate set consisting of Clifford+[MATH]. In particular, there are catalytic constant [MATH]-depth circuits that approximate multi-qubit Toffoli, adder, and quantum Fourier transform arbitrarily well. We also show that the catalyst state can be prepared in time polynomial in [MATH].

.
tldr: Shows that any single-qubit z-rotation can be executed in constant T-depth using a catalyst state of polynomial size, enabling constant-T-depth approximation of Toffoli, adder, and quantum Fourier transform.
motivation: Reducing T-depth is essential for practical fault-tolerant quantum computing, but single-qubit z-rotations typically demand long T-depth sequences; catalytic resource transformations may circumvent this limitation.
method: Uses catalytic quantum transformations to construct a catalyst state that enables constant T-depth z-rotations, proves the catalyst can be prepared in polynomial time, and applies the result to build a finite universal gate set.
result: The T-depth of any single-qubit z-rotation is reduced to constant with a catalyst state of size polynomial in 1/epsilon, yielding constant T-depth implementations of Toffoli, adder, and quantum Fourier transform.

title: Entanglement-assisted Quasi-cyclic Quantum Low-density Parity-check Codes Over Qubits
authors: Pavan Kumar, Abhi Kumar Sharma, Karthik Bharadwaj, And Shayan Srinivasa Garani
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2181 (2026).

We construct several families of entanglement-assisted quasi-cyclic quantum LDPC (EA-QC-QLDPC) codes via structured tilings of permutation matrices. The entanglement-unassisted portion of the joint Tanner graph of the proposed EA-QC-QLDPC code derived from two distinct classical QC-LDPC codes is free of 4-cycles. Notably, one of the proposed families constructed from two distinct classical codes requires only a [MATH] shared Bell pair between the quantum transmitter and receiver, highlighting its resource efficiency. We also analytically determine the exact code rates for some of the proposed constructions. Furthermore, two of the proposed families of EA-QC-QLDPC codes are derived from a single classical code whose Tanner graphs possess girth greater than six, further enhancing their error-correcting performance. We also propose an encoding scheme with improved complexity by exploiting the proposed code structure. The performance of the proposed codes is assessed under both random and burst error models under the depolarizing and Markovian noise actions. Simulation results reveal nearly one order of improvement in error-correction performance with the quaternary block-layered normalized min-sum (QBLNMS) decoder compared to the layered binary sum-product decoder over both depolarizing and Markovian channels. Using the QBLNMS decoder over a quaternary alphabet, we demonstrate that correlated Pauli errors can be effectively handled within the decoding framework. Furthermore, under the QBLNMS decoding, the proposed codes achieve [MATH] performance improvements compared to prior works and can effectively handle both random and burst errors. The code constructions are scalable across various coding rates and quantum payloads, crucial for practical quantum communication and computing systems.

.
tldr: The paper constructs entanglement-assisted quasi-cyclic quantum LDPC codes with improved decoding performance and resource efficiency for quantum communication and computing.
motivation: Quantum LDPC codes are promising for fault-tolerant quantum information processing, but constructing high-performance codes with low entanglement cost and efficient decoding remains challenging.
method: The authors design families of EA-QC-QLDPC codes using structured tilings of permutation matrices from classical QC-LDPC codes, ensuring the entanglement-unassisted Tanner graph is free of 4-cycles, and propose a quaternary block-layered normalized min-sum decoder.
result: Some families require only one shared Bell pair, achieve analytically determined code rates, and show nearly an order of magnitude improvement over layered binary sum-product decoding under depolarizing and Markovian noise, effectively handling random and burst errors.
conclusion: The proposed codes are scalable across coding rates and quantum payloads, offering practical advantages for quantum communication and computing systems.

title: Quantum Resource Comparison For Two Leading Surface Code Lattice Surgery Approaches
authors: Tyler Leblond And Ryan S. Bennink
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2187 (2026).

Hamiltonian simulation is one of the most promising candidates for the demonstration of quantum advantage within the next ten years, and several studies have proposed end-to-end resource estimates for executing such algorithms on fault-tolerant quantum processors. Usually, these resource estimates are based upon the assumption that quantum error correction is implemented using the surface code, and that the best surface code compilation scheme involves serializing input circuits by eliminating all Clifford gates. This transformation is thought to make best use of the native multi-body measurement (lattice surgery) instruction set available to surface codes. Some work, however, has suggested that direct compilation from Clifford+T to lattice surgery operations may be beneficial for circuits that have high degrees of logical parallelism. In this study, we analyze the resource costs for implementing Hamiltonian simulation using example approaches from each of these leading surface code compilation families. The Hamiltonians whose dynamics we consider are those of the transverse-field Ising model in several geometries, the Kitaev honeycomb model, and the [MATH] complex under a time-varying magnetic field. We show, among other things, that the optimal scheme depends on whether Hamiltonian simulation is implemented using the quantum signal processing or Trotter-Suzuki algorithms, with Trotterization benefiting by orders of magnitude from direct Clifford+T compilation for these applications. Our results suggest that surface code quantum computers should not have a one-size-fits-all compilation scheme, but that smart compilers should predict the optimal scheme based upon high-level quantities from logical circuits such as average circuit density, numbers of logical qubits, and T fraction.

.
tldr: The paper compares resource costs of two surface code lattice surgery compilation schemes for Hamiltonian simulation, finding that the optimal scheme depends on the algorithm and circuit parallelism.
motivation: Fault-tolerant resource estimates for Hamiltonian simulation typically assume serializing Clifford gates before lattice surgery, but direct Clifford+T compilation may benefit highly parallel circuits.
method: The authors analyze resource costs for Hamiltonian simulation of transverse-field Ising models, the Kitaev honeycomb model, and a complex under time-varying magnetic field, using both quantum signal processing and Trotter-Suzuki algorithms under two leading surface code compilation families.
result: Trotterization benefits by orders of magnitude from direct Clifford+T compilation for the studied applications, while the optimal scheme depends on high-level circuit quantities such as average circuit density, number of logical qubits, and T fraction.
conclusion: Surface code quantum computers should not use a one-size-fits-all compilation scheme; smart compilers should predict the optimal scheme based on logical circuit characteristics.

title: Promise Of Graph Sparsification And Decomposition For Noise Reduction In Qaoa: Analysis For Trapped-Ion Compilations
authors: Jai Moondra, Phillip C. Lotshaw, Greg Mohler, And Swati Gupta
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2185 (2026).

We develop new approximate compilation schemes that significantly reduce the expense of compiling the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) for solving the Max-Cut problem. Our main focus is on compilation with trapped-ion simulators using Pauli-[MATH] operations and all-to-all Ising Hamiltonian [MATH] evolution generated by Molmer-Sorensen or optical dipole force interactions, though some of our results also apply to standard gate-based compilations. Our results are based on principles of graph sparsification and decomposition; the former reduces the number of edges in a graph while maintaining its cut structure, while the latter breaks a weighted graph into a small number of unweighted graphs. Though these techniques have been used as heuristics in various hybrid quantum algorithms, there have been no guarantees on their performance, to the best of our knowledge. This work provides the first provable guarantees using sparsification and decomposition to improve quantum noise resilience and reduce quantum circuit complexity. For quantum hardware that uses edge-by-edge QAOA compilations, sparsification leads to a direct reduction in circuit complexity. For trapped-ion quantum simulators implementing all-to-all [MATH] pulses, we show that for a [MATH] factor loss in the Max-Cut approximation ([MATH], our compilations improve the (worst-case) number of [MATH] pulses from [MATH] to [MATH] and the (worst-case) number of Pauli-[MATH] bit flips from [MATH] to [MATH] for [MATH]-node graphs. This is an asymptotic improvement for any constant [MATH]. We demonstrate that significant improvements to the approximation ratio are obtained using decomposition in simulated trapped-ion experiments with dephasing noise. We further present a generic argument showing that sparsification results in an exponentially improved circuit fidelity lower bound in digital computing schemes based on one- and two-qubit gates, which are relevant to a wide variety of hardwares such as superconducting qubits and certain neutral atom or trapped ion setups, and more sophisticated noise models. We anticipate these approximate compilation techniques will be useful tools in a variety of future quantum computing experiments.

.
tldr: New approximate compilation schemes based on graph sparsification and decomposition significantly reduce circuit complexity and improve noise resilience for QAOA Max-Cut on trapped-ion and gate-based quantum hardware.
motivation: Compiling QAOA for Max-Cut is expensive, especially on trapped-ion simulators using all-to-all Ising interactions, and existing sparsification/decomposition heuristics lack performance guarantees.
method: The authors provide provable guarantees for sparsification and decomposition in QAOA compilation, analyzing trapped-ion Pauli-X and Mølmer-Sørensen pulse counts, and deriving a generic fidelity lower bound for digital gate-based compilations.
result: For a constant-factor loss in Max-Cut approximation, the number of MS pulses and Pauli-X flips is asymptotically reduced for n-node graphs; simulated trapped-ion experiments with dephasing show improved approximation ratios.
conclusion: These approximate compilation techniques are promising tools for reducing noise and resource overhead in future quantum computing experiments across multiple hardware platforms.

title: Efficient Graph State Generation In Linear Optics
authors: Seungbeom Chin And William John Munro
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2189 (2026).

Graph states are central resources for quantum information processing, supporting applications in computation, communication, and error correction. In photonic systems, they are typically assembled from smaller entangled states using probabilistic fusion gates, which demand many photons and suffer from low success rates. We present an optimized scheme for directly generating caterpillar graph states (CGSs)—essential resource states for constructing high-dimensional lattice graph states—using only single-photon sources, linear optics, and heralded measurements. Based on the linear quantum graph (LQG) picture, our method produces CGSs efficiently. For CGSs of length [MATH], it requires [MATH] fewer photons and achieves a success rate [MATH] times higher than fusion-based approaches. These results demonstrate that the LQG picture provides a powerful and flexible route to generating complex photonic graph states for efficient quantum information processing.

.
tldr: The paper presents an optimized linear-optics scheme for directly generating caterpillar graph states using single-photon sources, linear optics, and heralded measurements, achieving fewer photons and higher success rates than fusion-based methods.
motivation: Graph states are key resources for quantum computation, communication, and error correction, but photonic generation via probabilistic fusion gates is resource-intensive and inefficient.
method: Based on the linear quantum graph (LQG) picture, they design an optimized linear-optics circuit that uses single-photon sources, beam splitters, phase shifters, and photon-number-resolving detectors to directly generate caterpillar graph states with high fidelity and success probability.

title: Faster Quantum Simulation Of Markovian Open Quantum Systems Via Randomisation
authors: I.J. David, I. Sinayskiy, And F. Petruccione
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2204 (2026).

When simulating the dynamics of open quantum systems with quantum computers, it is essential to accurately approximate the system's behaviour while preserving the physicality of its evolution. Traditionally, for Markovian open quantum systems, this has been achieved using first and second-order Trotter-Suzuki product formulas or probabilistic algorithms. In this work, we introduce novel non-probabilistic algorithms for simulating Markovian open quantum systems using randomisation. Our methods, including first and second-order randomised Trotter-Suzuki formulas and the QDRIFT channel, not only maintain the physicality of the system's evolution but also enhance the scalability and precision of quantum simulations. We derive error bounds and step count limits for these techniques, bypassing the need for the mixing lemma typically employed in Hamiltonian simulation proofs. Furthermore, we implement these randomised algorithms using Classical Sampling (CS), demonstrating their gate complexity advantages over deterministic TS product formulas. This work systematically extends powerful randomisation techniques from Hamiltonian simulation to the general setting of Markovian open quantum systems, highlighting their potential to enable faster and more accurate simulations.

.
tldr: The paper introduces randomised algorithms (first- and second-order randomised Trotter-Suzuki and QDRIFT channel) for faster quantum simulation of Markovian open quantum systems while preserving physicality.
motivation: Simulating open quantum system dynamics on quantum computers requires accurate and efficient methods that maintain complete positivity, and existing deterministic Trotter-Suzuki formulas can be improved via randomisation techniques successfully used in Hamiltonian simulation.
method: The authors extend randomised Trotter-Suzuki and QDRIFT to Markovian open quantum systems, derive error bounds and step count limits without the mixing lemma, and implement the algorithms using Classical Sampling (CS).
result: The randomised algorithms achieve better gate complexity than deterministic Trotter-Suzuki product formulas and preserve the physicality of the evolution, as demonstrated through error analysis and complexity comparisons.
conclusion: Randomisation provides a systematic route to faster and more accurate quantum simulation of Markovian open quantum systems, extending randomisation techniques from Hamiltonian simulation to the open-system setting.

title: Reducing Spatial And Temporal Dimensionality In The Multidimensional Caldeira-Leggett Model
authors: Hongfei Zhan, Ernest W.Z. Pan, And Zhenning Cai
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2201 (2026).

Focusing on the real-time dynamics of the reduced density matrix of the multidimensional Caldeira-Leggett model, several techniques are adopted in this paper to reduce the spatial and temporal dimensionality, combined into an efficient algorithm. From a spatial perspective, an equivalent formulation of the Dyson series is presented. With the aid of a low-rank approximation, the spatial dimensionality of open quantum system simulations is halved. From a temporal perspective, the frozen Gaussian approximation is used to approximate both the evolution operator and the interaction operator in the multidimensional Caldeira-Leggett model. This reduces the high-dimensional integrals to one- and two-dimensional integrals independent of the truncation level of the Dyson series. Through these techniques, we design an efficient algorithm whose validity is verified through several numerical experiments, including a two-dimensional double slit simulation.

.
tldr: The paper introduces an efficient algorithm for simulating real-time dynamics of the multidimensional Caldeira-Leggett model by reducing spatial and temporal dimensionality via low-rank and frozen Gaussian approximations.
motivation: Simulating open quantum systems in high dimensions is computationally demanding, and the Caldeira-Leggett model is a paradigmatic testbed for quantum dissipation and decoherence.
method: The authors present an equivalent Dyson series formulation and use a low-rank approximation to halve spatial dimensionality, while the frozen Gaussian approximation reduces high-dimensional integrals to one- and two-dimensional integrals independent of the Dyson series truncation level.
result: Numerical experiments, including a two-dimensional double-slit simulation, demonstrate the validity and efficiency of the proposed algorithm.
conclusion: The approach offers a promising numerical tool for multidimensional open quantum system dynamics, though its direct relevance to information-theoretic thermodynamics remains indirect.

title: Robust Topological Quantum State Transfer With Long-range Interactions In Rydberg Arrays
authors: Siri Raupach, Beatriz Olmos, And Mathias B. M. Svendsen
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2190 (2026).

We develop a theoretical framework for fast, robust and high-fidelity topological quantum state transfer in one-dimensional systems with long-range couplings, motivated by chains of Rydberg atoms with dipole–dipole interactions. Such long-range interactions naturally give rise to extended Su–Schrieffer–Heeger and Rice–Mele models supporting topologically protected edge states. We show that these edge states enable high-fidelity edge-to-edge excitation transfer using both time-independent protocols, based on coherent edge state dynamics, and time-dependent protocols, based on adiabatic modulation of system parameters. Long-range couplings play a central role by enhancing the relevant energy gaps, leading to a substantial improvement in transfer efficiency compared to nearest neighbour models. The resulting transfer is robust against positional disorder, reflecting its topological origin and highlighting the potential of long-range interacting platforms for reliable quantum state transfer.

.
tldr: A theoretical framework for fast, robust topological quantum state transfer along edge states in long-range-coupled Rydberg atom chains, using both coherent and adiabatic protocols.
motivation: Reliable quantum state transfer is essential for distributed quantum information processing, and Rydberg arrays with dipole-dipole interactions offer a natural platform whose long-range couplings may enhance topological protection.
method: The authors derive extended Su-Schrieffer-Heeger and Rice-Mele models for one-dimensional dipolar Rydberg chains, then analyze edge-to-edge excitation transfer via time-independent coherent edge-state dynamics and time-dependent adiabatic parameter modulation.
result: Long-range couplings enlarge the relevant topological energy gaps, yielding substantially higher transfer fidelity than nearest-neighbour models, with robustness against positional disorder due to the topological origin of the edge states.
conclusion: Long-range interacting Rydberg platforms are promising for reliable, disorder-robust topological quantum state transfer, motivating further exploration of driven and longer-chain configurations.

title: Disorder-Induced Entanglement Phase Transitions In Non-Hermitian Systems With Skin Effects
authors: Kai Li, Ze-Chuan Liu, And Yong Xu
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2186 (2026).

Non-Hermitian dynamics is ubiquitous in various physical systems. While recent study shows that such a dynamics leads to an area-law scaling of the entanglement entropy due to the non-Hermitian skin effects, it remains unclear how disorder changes the behavior of the entanglement entropy in a non-Hermitian system with skin effects. Here we study the dynamics of a many-body state of free fermions in the paradigmatic Hatano-Nelson model with open boundaries, and find that the area-law behavior of the entanglement entropy in the pristine Hatano-Nelson model develops into a logarithmic scaling for small disorder strength. As we further increase the disorder strength, the system reenters an area-law regime through an entanglement phase transition. At the critical point, the entanglement entropy exhibits a universal algebraic scaling. We further demonstrate the absence of a conformal invariance in the log-law regime by examining the subsystem entanglement entropy, the connected correlation function and the mutual information. Finally, we show the existence of disorder induced entanglement phase transitions in the Hatano-Nelson model with periodic boundaries.

.
tldr: Disorder drives a sequence of entanglement phase transitions in the non-Hermitian Hatano-Nelson model, turning area-law behavior into logarithmic scaling and back into an area law with universal algebraic scaling at criticality.
motivation: While the non-Hermitian skin effect is known to induce area-law entanglement scaling, it was unclear how disorder modifies entanglement entropy in such non-Hermitian systems with skin effects.
method: The authors simulate the dynamics of a many-body free-fermion state in the Hatano-Nelson model with open (and periodic) boundaries, tuning disorder strength and analyzing subsystem entanglement entropy, connected correlation functions, and mutual information.
result: Small disorder converts the pristine area law into a logarithmic scaling regime that lacks conformal invariance, while stronger disorder reenters an area-law phase through an entanglement phase transition, with universal algebraic scaling at the critical point.
conclusion: Disorder-induced entanglement phase transitions occur in non-Hermitian skin-effect systems for both open and periodic boundaries, extending non-Hermitian entanglement phenomenology beyond the clean area-law picture.

title: Unconditional Quantum Advantage For Sampling With Shallow Circuits
authors: Adam Bene Watts And Natalie Parham
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2188 (2026).

Recent work by Bravyi, Gosset, and Koenig showed that there exists a search problem that a constant-depth quantum circuit can solve, but that any constant-depth classical circuit with bounded fan-in cannot. They also pose the question: Can we achieve a similar proof of separation for an input-independent sampling task? In this paper, we show that the answer to this question is yes when the number of random input bits given to the classical circuit is bounded. We introduce a distribution [MATH] over [MATH] and construct a constant-depth uniform quantum circuit family [MATH] such that [MATH] samples from a distribution close to [MATH] in total variation distance. For any [MATH] we also prove, unconditionally, that any classical circuit with bounded fan-in gates that takes as input [MATH] i.i.d. Bernouli random variables with entropy [MATH] and produces output close to [MATH] in total variation distance has depth [MATH]. This gives an unconditional proof that constant-depth quantum circuits can sample from distributions that can't be reproduced by constant-depth bounded fan-in classical circuits, even up to additive error. We also show a similar separation between constant-depth quantum circuits with advice and classical circuits with bounded fan-in and fan-out, but access to an unbounded number of i.i.d random inputs. The distribution [MATH] and classical circuit lower bounds are inspired by work of Viola, in which he shows a different (but related) distribution cannot be sampled from approximately by constant-depth bounded fan-in classical circuits.

.
tldr: Constant-depth quantum circuits can sample from a distribution that no constant-depth bounded fan-in classical circuit with limited random input bits can reproduce, yielding an unconditional quantum advantage for a shallow-circuit sampling task.
motivation: Bravyi, Gosset, and Koenig previously showed a search-problem separation for constant-depth circuits and asked whether a similar separation could be proven for an input-independent sampling task.
method: The authors introduce a distribution over bit strings, construct a uniform constant-depth quantum circuit family that samples close to it in total variation distance, and prove unconditional lower bounds for classical bounded fan-in circuits using techniques inspired by Viola.
result: They prove that for any accuracy, classical circuits with bounded fan-in gates and access to i.i.d. Bernoulli random variables of bounded entropy require depth growing with the input size, even up to additive error; a similar separation is shown for quantum circuits with advice versus classical circuits with bounded fan-in/fan-out and unbounded random inputs.
conclusion: The work answers the open question affirmatively for the bounded-random-input setting and establishes a new unconditional sampling-based separation between shallow quantum and classical circuits.

title: Non-Gaussian Noise Magnetometry Using Local Spin Qubits
authors: Jonathan B. Curtis, Amir Yacoby, And Eugene Demler
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2197 (2026).

Atomic scale qubits, as may be realized in nitrogen vacancy (NV) centers in diamond, offer the opportunity to study magnetic field noise with nanometer scale spatial resolution. Using these spin qubits, one can learn a great deal about the magnetic-field noise correlations, and correspondingly the collective-mode spectra, in quantum materials and devices. However, to date these tools have been essentially restricted to studying Gaussian noise processes – equivalent to linear-response. In this work we will show how to extend these techniques beyond the Gaussian regime and show how to unambiguously measure higher-order magnetic noise cumulants in a local, spatially resolved way. We unveil two protocols for doing this; the first uses a single spin-qubit and different dynamical decoupling sequences to extract non-Markovian and non-Gaussian spin-echo noise. The second protocol uses two-qubit coincidence measurements to study spatially non-local cumulants in the magnetic noise. We then demonstrate the utility of these protocols by considering a model of a bath of non-interacting two-level systems, as well as a model involving spatially correlated magnetic fluctuations near a second-order Ising phase transition. In both cases, we highlight how this technique can be used to measure in a real many-body system how fluctuation dynamics converge towards the central limit theorem as a function of effective bath size. We then conclude by discussing some promising applications and extensions of this method.

.
tldr: The paper develops protocols using single and two-qubit NV-center spin sensors to measure higher-order (non-Gaussian) magnetic noise cumulants with nanoscale spatial resolution.
motivation: Existing spin-qubit magnetometry tools are restricted to Gaussian noise processes, equivalent to linear response, leaving non-Gaussian and non-Markovian magnetic fluctuations in materials uncharacterized.
method: Two protocols are proposed: one uses a single spin qubit with tailored dynamical decoupling sequences to extract non-Markovian and non-Gaussian spin-echo noise cumulants, and another uses two-qubit coincidence measurements to access spatially non-local noise cumulants. These are applied to a bath of non-interacting two-level systems and to spatially correlated magnetic fluctuations near a second-order Ising transition.
result: The protocols unambiguously extract higher-order magnetic noise cumulants locally and show how fluctuation dynamics converge toward the central limit theorem as a function of effective bath size in real many-body systems.
conclusion: The work extends NV-based magnetometry beyond the Gaussian/linear-response regime and outlines promising applications and extensions for probing collective-mode spectra in quantum materials.

title: Quantum Max d-Cut Via Qudit Swap Operators
authors: Igor Klep, Tea Štrekelj, And Jurij Volčič
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2203 (2026).

Quantum Max Cut (QMC) problem for systems of qubits is an example of a 2-local Hamiltonian problem, and a prominent paradigm in computational complexity theory. This paper investigates the algebraic structure of a higher-dimensional analog of the QMC problem for systems of qudits. The Quantum Max [MATH]-Cut ([MATH]-QMC) problem asks for the largest eigenvalue of a Hamiltonian on a graph with [MATH] vertices whose edges correspond to swap operators acting on [MATH]. The algebra generated by the swap operators is identified as a quotient of a free algebra modulo symmetric group relations and a single additional relation of degree [MATH]. This presentation leads to a tailored hierarchy of semidefinite programs, leveraging noncommutative polynomial optimization (NPO) methods, that converges to the solution of the [MATH]-QMC problem. For a large class of complete bipartite graphs, exact solutions for the [MATH]-QMC problem are derived using the representation theory of symmetric groups and Littlewood-Richardson coefficients. Lastly, the paper addresses a refined [MATH]-QMC problem focused on finding the largest eigenvalue within each isotypic component (irreducible block) of the graph Hamiltonian. It is shown that the spectrum of the star graph Hamiltonian distinguishes between isotypic components of the [MATH]-QMC problem. For general [MATH], low-degree relations for separating isotypic components are presented, enabling adaptation of the global NPO hierarchy to efficiently compute the largest eigenvalue in each isotypic component.

.
tldr: The paper studies the algebraic structure of a higher-dimensional Quantum Max Cut problem for qudits, using swap operators to derive a semidefinite programming hierarchy and exact solutions for complete bipartite graphs.
motivation: Quantum Max Cut is a prominent 2-local Hamiltonian problem in computational complexity, and its qudit generalization is less understood algebraically.
method: The authors identify the algebra generated by qudit swap operators as a quotient of a free algebra, then use noncommutative polynomial optimization and representation theory (symmetric groups, Littlewood-Richardson coefficients) to build tailored SDP hierarchies.
result: They obtain exact solutions for a large class of complete bipartite graphs and show that low-degree relations can separate isotypic components, enabling efficient computation of the largest eigenvalue in each block.
conclusion: The work provides an algebraic and optimization framework for the Quantum Max d-Cut problem, with potential for computing spectral properties of graph Hamiltonians via semidefinite programming.

title: Quantum Phase Estimation With Optimal Confidence Interval Using Three Control Qubits
authors: Kaur Kristjuhan And Dominic W. Berry
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2193 (2026).

Quantum phase estimation is an important routine in many quantum algorithms, particularly for estimating the ground state energy in quantum chemistry simulations. This estimation involves applying powers of a unitary to the ground state, controlled by an auxiliary state prepared on a control register. In many applications the goal is to provide a confidence interval for the phase estimate, and optimal performance is provided by a discrete prolate spheroidal sequence. We show how to prepare the corresponding state in a far more efficient way than prior work. We find that a matrix product state representation with a bond dimension of 4 is sufficient to give a highly accurate approximation for all dimensions tested, up to [MATH]. This matrix product state can be efficiently prepared using a sequence of simple three-qubit operations. When the dimension is a power of 2, the phase estimation can be performed with only three qubits for the control register, making it suitable for early-generation fault-tolerant quantum computers with a limited number of logical qubits.

﻿

.
tldr: The paper presents an efficient matrix product state preparation of the optimal control state for quantum phase estimation, requiring only three control qubits.
motivation: Quantum phase estimation is crucial for quantum chemistry simulations, but preparing the optimal state for a desired confidence interval is challenging and resource-intensive.
method: They approximate the discrete prolate spheroidal sequence with a matrix product state of bond dimension 4 and prepare it using a sequence of simple three-qubit operations.
result: The approach achieves high accuracy for all tested dimensions up to large sizes, and when the dimension is a power of 2, the control register needs only three qubits.
conclusion: This makes quantum phase estimation feasible on early fault-tolerant quantum computers with limited logical qubits.

title: On The Quantum Computational Complexity Of Classical Linear Dynamics With Geometrically Local Interactions: Dequantization And Universality
authors: Kazuki Sakamoto And Keisuke Fujii
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2182 (2026).

The simulation of large-scale classical systems in exponentially small space on quantum computers has gained attention. The prior work demonstrated that a quantum algorithm offers an exponential speedup over any classical algorithm in simulating classical dynamics with long-range interactions. However, many real-world classical systems, such as those arising from partial differential equations, exhibit only local interactions. The question remains whether quantum algorithms can still provide exponential speedup under this condition. In this work, we thoroughly characterize the computational complexity of simulating such geometrically local systems on quantum computers. First, we dequantize the quantum algorithm for simulating short-time (polynomial-time) dynamics of such systems. This implies that the problem of simulating this dynamics does not yield any exponential quantum advantage. Second, we show that simulating short-time dynamics is at least as hard as polynomial-time and linear-space probabilistic classical computation. Third, we show that the computational complexity of simulating long-time (exponential-time) dynamics is captured by exponential-time and polynomial-space quantum computation. This suggests a super-polynomial time advantage when restricting the computation to polynomial-space, or an exponential space advantage otherwise. This work offers new insights into the complexity of classical dynamics governed by partial differential equations, providing a pathway for achieving quantum advantage in practical problems.

.
tldr: The paper characterizes the quantum computational complexity of simulating geometrically local classical linear dynamics, showing dequantization for short-time dynamics and quantum universality for long-time dynamics.
motivation: Prior work demonstrated exponential quantum speedup for classical dynamics with long-range interactions, but it was unclear whether such advantage persists when interactions are geometrically local, as in many PDE-based systems.
method: The authors dequantize a quantum algorithm for short-time dynamics, prove hardness results relative to probabilistic classical computation, and analyze long-time dynamics through the lens of exponential-time polynomial-space quantum computation.
result: Short-time simulation admits no exponential quantum advantage and is at least as hard as polynomial-time linear-space probabilistic classical computation, while long-time simulation is captured by exponential-time polynomial-space quantum computation.
conclusion: The results clarify the complexity landscape of classical dynamics governed by PDEs, indicating that quantum advantages may only arise for long-time evolution or under space restrictions.

title: Measuring Universal Magnetocaloric Scaling Functions Near Quantum Critical Point
authors: Junsen Xiang, Enze Lv, Qinxin Shen, Cheng Su, Xuetong He, Yinghao Zhu, Yuan Gao, Xin-Yang Liu, Dai-Wei Qu, Xinlei Wang, Xi Chen, Qian Zhao, Haifeng Li, Shuo Li, Jie Yang, Jun Luo, Wentao Jin, Yang Qi, Rui Zhou, Wei Li, Peijie Sun And Gang Su
abstract: Near a quantum critical point (QCP), the low-temperature thermodynamics follows universal scaling laws. Using copper sulfate pentahydrate—a canonical spin-1/2 antiferromagnetic Heisenberg chain compound—we report the observation of a universal magnetocaloric effect (MCE) near a field-driven QCP. Remarkably, in the 1D quantum-critical regime, we obtain the universal magnetocaloric scaling function via adiabatic demagnetization measurements, which agrees with the analytical solution of the critical 1D Fermi gas. This establishes the copper sulfate crystal as an ideal platform for studying quantum criticality and universal phenomena. Upon further cooling, our MCE and nuclear magnetic resonance measurements reveal a dimensional crossover to a 3D quantum-critical regime of the Bose–Einstein condensation (BEC) universality class, characterized by the scaling law and a clear data collapse of the magnetic Grüneisen ratio with the 3D Bose-gas scaling function . Practically, this quantum-critical MCE enables cooling to 68.7 mK near the QCP and achieves a lowest temperature of 12.8 mK at zero field without the need for helium-3. Our work identifies a universal MCE in a common compound, establishing this magnon BEC system as a prototype quantum-critical coolant and a platform for next-generation millikelvin refrigeration.
tldr: The paper reports universal magnetocaloric scaling near a field-driven quantum critical point in copper sulfate, enabling millikelvin cooling without helium-3.
motivation: Quantum critical points host universal thermodynamics, but measuring universal scaling functions and exploiting them for practical cooling remains challenging.
method: Adiabatic demagnetization, magnetocaloric effect, and nuclear magnetic resonance measurements on a spin-1/2 antiferromagnetic Heisenberg chain compound, compared with analytical 1D Fermi gas and 3D Bose-Einstein condensation scaling functions.
result: A universal magnetocaloric scaling function is observed in the 1D quantum-critical regime, with a dimensional crossover to 3D BEC universality class, achieving cooling to 68.7 mK near the QCP and 12.8 mK at zero field.
conclusion: Copper sulfate pentahydrate is established as a prototype quantum-critical coolant and a platform for next-generation millikelvin refrigeration without helium-3.

title: Transverse Geometry Reshapes Current And Tracer Fluctuation Amplitudes In Quasi-one-dimensional Single Files
authors: Olivier Bénichou And Aurélien Grabsch
abstract: Single-file transport means no overtaking: particles move in a narrow channel while preserving their longitudinal order. This simple constraint has profound dynamical consequences, most notably tracer subdiffusion, and has made single-file transport a paradigmatic form of confined many-body motion, observed from molecular transport in zeolites to single-file diffusion of colloids in narrow channels. A common modelling approach assumes that, once overtaking is suppressed, finite-width effects can be discarded or represented by an effective particle size in a strictly one-dimensional model. Starting from the Brownian dynamics in the full confined geometry, we instead derive the exact large-scale one-dimensional fluctuating-hydrodynamic equation governing the coarse-grained line density. Its transport coefficients are fixed by the confined equilibrium equation of state, through which the transverse geometry remains encoded in the one-dimensional description. Consequently, transverse geometry leaves the single-file scaling unchanged but can qualitatively reshape the density dependence of the current and tracer fluctuation amplitudes. In the minimal hard-core setting, this yields a collective diffusivity that can become non-monotonic in density for sufficiently wide no-passing channels. This geometric non-monotonicity propagates to exact large-scale predictions for the amplitudes of integrated-current fluctuations and tracer-displacement fluctuations. The effect is robust to the interaction potential, channel geometry, initial preparation and microscopic dynamics. Quasi-one-dimensional single-file transport therefore defines a distinct regime in which forbidding overtaking does not erase geometry from collective transport.
tldr: The paper derives an exact one-dimensional fluctuating-hydrodynamic description of single-file transport that encodes transverse geometry via the confined equilibrium equation of state, showing geometry can reshape density dependence of current and tracer fluctuation amplitudes.
motivation: Single-file transport is often modeled as an effective 1D system where finite-width effects are ignored or reduced to an effective particle size, but the role of transverse geometry in large-scale transport properties remains unclear. This work addresses this gap by deriving an exact 1D fluctuating hydrodynamics that accounts for transverse geometry through the equilibrium equation of state, enabling predictions for how confinement geometry affects density dependence of current and tracer fluctuations.

title: Universally Diverging Grüneisen Ratio Of Holographic Quantum Criticality
authors: Jun-Kun Zhao, Enze Lv, Wei Li And Li Li
abstract: Quantum criticality is a hallmark of strongly correlated electron systems, as seen in heavy-fermion materials and high-temperature superconductors. Holographic duality provides a powerful framework to investigate these systems by translating them into weakly coupled classical gravity living in one higher dimension. Here, we exploit this approach to study a field-induced quantum critical point with dynamical exponent in Einstein–Maxwell–Chern–Simons theory. Our analysis of its thermodynamic properties reveals a new universality class. Notably, we identify a diverging Grüneisen ratio with universal scaling , a behavior that closely mirrors recent experiments on the heavy-fermion material CeRh Ge . These findings advance our understanding of metallic quantum criticality and highlight the potential of holographic duality as a powerful tool for studying correlated quantum matter as well as its magnetocaloric applications.
tldr: Using holographic duality, the paper studies a field-induced quantum critical point and finds a universally diverging Grüneisen ratio that matches heavy-fermion experiments.
motivation: Quantum criticality in strongly correlated electron systems is challenging, and holographic duality offers a way to map it to classical gravity, potentially revealing universal thermodynamic behavior.
method: Analyze thermodynamic properties of a field-induced quantum critical point with dynamical exponent in Einstein–Maxwell–Chern–Simons theory.
result: Identify a new universality class with a diverging Grüneisen ratio showing universal scaling, closely mirroring recent experiments on CeRhGe.
conclusion: Advances understanding of metallic quantum criticality and highlights holographic duality for correlated quantum matter and magnetocaloric applications.

title: Sparse Quantum State Preparation With Improved Toffoli Cost
authors: Felix Rupprecht And Sabine Wölk
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2208 (2026).

The preparation of quantum states is one of the most fundamental tasks in quantum computing, and a key primitive in many quantum algorithms. Of particular interest to areas such as quantum simulation and linear-system solvers are sparse quantum states, which contain only a small number [MATH] of non-zero computational basis states compared to a generic state. In this work, we present an approach that prepares [MATH]-sparse states on [MATH] qubits, reducing the number of Toffoli gates required compared to prior art. We work in the established framework of first preparing a dense state on a [MATH]-qubit sub-register, and then mapping this state to the target state via an isometry, with the latter step dominating the cost of the full algorithm. The speed-up is achieved by designing an efficient algorithm for finding and implementing the isometry. The worst-case Toffoli cost of our isometry circuit, which may be viewed as a batched version of an approach by Malvetti et al., is essentially [MATH] for sufficiently large values of [MATH], yielding roughly a [MATH] improvement factor over the state-of-the-art. In numerical benchmarks on randomly chosen states, the cost is closer to [MATH]. With the improved isometry circuit, we examine the dense-state preparation step and present ways to optimize the joint cost of both steps, particularly in the case of target states with purely real coefficients, by outsourcing some sub-tasks from the dense-state preparation to the isometry.

.
tldr: The paper presents an improved method for preparing sparse quantum states on a quantum computer, reducing the number of Toffoli gates needed compared to prior art.
motivation: Sparse quantum state preparation is a fundamental primitive for quantum simulation and linear-system solvers, but existing methods have high circuit cost dominated by the isometry step.
method: The approach first prepares a dense state on a small sub-register and then applies an efficiently found and implemented isometry to map it to the target sparse state, with optimizations for real coefficients.
result: The worst-case Toffoli cost is essentially optimal up to polylog factors, yielding roughly a square-root improvement over the state of the art, and numerical benchmarks on random states show even lower costs.
conclusion: The improved isometry circuit significantly reduces the Toffoli cost of sparse state preparation, offering a practical speedup for quantum algorithms relying on such states.

title: A Brief History Of Quantum Vs Classical Computational Advantage
authors: Ryan Larose
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2198 (2026).

In this review article we summarize all experiments claiming quantum computational advantage to date. Our review highlights challenges, loopholes, and refutations appearing in subsequent work to provide a complete picture of the current statuses of these experiments. In addition, we also discuss theoretical computational advantage in example problems such as approximate optimization and recommendation systems. Finally, we review recent experiments in quantum error correction --- the biggest frontier to reach experimental quantum advantage in Shor's algorithm.

.
tldr: A review cataloguing all experiments claiming quantum computational advantage, plus their subsequent challenges/refutations, along with theoretical advantage problems and error-correction milestones.
motivation: The claimed demonstrations of quantum computational advantage have accumulated loopholes and rebuttals, so a consolidated critical survey is needed to clarify the true status of these experiments.
method: Survey/review methodology: systematic compilation and critical assessment of published quantum advantage experiments, their critiques, and refutations, alongside a discussion of theoretical advantage in approximate optimization and recommendation systems and recent QEC experiments.
result: The review organizes the landscape of quantum advantage claims, highlighting which results have been undermined or refuted and identifying quantum error correction as the key bottleneck for reaching advantage in Shor's algorithm.
conclusion: While experimental quantum advantage claims remain contested, progress in quantum error correction is identified as the critical frontier for achieving fault-tolerant, classically hard computation.

title: A Dynamical Lie-algebraic Framework For Hamiltonian Engineering And Quantum Control
authors: Yanying Liang, Ruibin Xu, Mao-Sheng Li, Haozhen Situ And Zhu-Jun Zheng
abstract: Determining the unitary dynamics accessible from finite Hamiltonian resources is a central problem in Hamiltonian engineering and quantum control. Dynamical Lie algebras (DLAs) connect available control Hamiltonians with the reachable dynamics, but their use as a design tool for modifying Hamiltonian generator sets remains less developed. In this work, we develop a finite-dimensional DLA framework for three generator-set operations: composition, invariance, and reduction. For composition, we construct direct sums of component DLAs using spectral projectors on an auxiliary register. For invariance, we analyze when modifications of Pauli-string generating sets preserve the generated Lie algebra, and introduce algebraic diagnostics for added generators. For reduction, we consider compact reductive DLAs and show how projection onto selected simple ideals gives reduced generating sets whose Lie closures are the corresponding ideal sums. We illustrate these results with finite-dimensional applications and numerical studies, including direct-sum dimension addition, central-spin invariance diagnostics, and the relation among DLA reduction, task relevance, and gradient behavior at finite system sizes. The results show how DLA structure can be used to diagnose controllability and guide Hamiltonian generator design under explicit algebraic assumptions.
tldr: The paper develops a finite-dimensional dynamical Lie algebra framework for composing, modifying, and reducing Hamiltonian generator sets to guide quantum control and Hamiltonian engineering.
motivation: Determining accessible unitary dynamics from limited Hamiltonian resources is central to quantum control, but DLA tools for designing generator sets remain underdeveloped.
method: It uses spectral projectors on an auxiliary register for direct sums, analyzes invariance of Pauli-string generating sets with algebraic diagnostics, and reduces compact reductive DLAs via projection onto simple ideals.
