result: The framework yields direct-sum dimension addition, central-spin invariance diagnostics, and links DLA reduction to task relevance and gradient behavior in finite-size numerical studies.
conclusion: DLA structure can diagnose controllability and guide Hamiltonian generator design under explicit algebraic assumptions, though applications remain within quantum control theory.

title: Solving The Nonlinear Vlasov Equation On A Quantum Computer
authors: Tamás Vaszary, Animesh Datta, Tom Goffrey, And Brian Appelbe
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2206 (2026).

The practical applicability of a recent Carleman-linearization-based quantum algorithm for solving ordinary differential equations (ODEs) with quadratic nonlinearities is investigated for the nonlinear electrostatic Vlasov equation with Krook-type collision operators. The equation is discretized on a (1+1)-dimensional phase-space grid and mapped onto the input of the quantum algorithm. Upper bounds for the query and gate complexities are derived in the limit of large grid sizes and found to be polynomially larger than the time complexity of the corresponding classical algorithms, primarily due to the dimension, sparsity, and norm of the Carleman-linearized evolution matrix. The convergence criteria are shown to impose severe restrictions on physically relevant plasma applications, requiring dissipation levels far exceeding those provided by the Krook operator.

.
tldr: Investigates the practical applicability of a Carleman-linearization-based quantum algorithm for solving the nonlinear electrostatic Vlasov equation, finding polynomial complexity overhead and severe convergence restrictions.
motivation: To assess whether quantum computers can efficiently solve nonlinear plasma physics equations relevant to fusion and astrophysics.
method: Discretizes the Vlasov equation with Krook-type collision operators on a (1+1)-dimensional phase-space grid and maps it to a Carleman-linearized quantum ODE solver, deriving query and gate complexity upper bounds.
result: The quantum algorithm's complexity is polynomially larger than classical algorithms due to the dimension, sparsity, and norm of the Carleman matrix, and convergence criteria require dissipation levels far exceeding those from the Krook operator.
conclusion: The current Carleman-linearization quantum algorithm is impractical for physically relevant plasma applications, highlighting the need for substantial algorithmic improvements.

title: On The Relation Between Perspective-neutral, Algebraic, And Effective Quantum Reference Frames
authors: Julian de Vuyst, Philipp A. Hoehn, And Artur Tsobanjan
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2196 (2026).

The framework of internal quantum reference frames (QRFs) constitutes a universal toolset for dealing with symmetries in quantum theory and has led to new revelations in quantum gravity, gauge theories and foundational physics. Multiple approaches have emerged, sometimes differing in scope and the way symmetries are implemented, raising the question as to their relation. Here, we investigate the relation between three approaches to QRFs for gauge symmetries, namely the [MATH] semiclassical, [MATH], and [MATH] (PN) approaches. Rather than constructing Hilbert spaces, as the PN approach, the effective approach is based on a quantum phase space parametrized by expectation values and fluctuations, while the emphasis of the algebraic approach is on the state space of complex linear functionals on a kinematical algebra. Nevertheless, external frame information is treated as gauge in all three formalisms, manifested in constraints on states and algebra. We show that these three approaches are, in fact, equivalent for ideal QRFs, distinguished by sharp orientations, which is the previous setting of the first two approaches. Our demonstration pertains to single constraints, including relativistic ones, and encompasses QRF changes. In particular, the QRF transformations of the PN framework agree semiclassically with those of the older effective approach, by which it was inspired. As a physical application, we explore the QRF covariance of uncertainties and fluctuations, which turn out to be frame dependent. This is particularly well-suited for the effective and algebraic approaches, for which these quantities form a natural basis. Finally, we pave the way towards extending these two approaches to non-ideal QRFs by studying the projection and gauge-fixing operations of the Page-Wootters formalism, built into the PN framework, on algebraic states.

.
tldr: The paper proves equivalence between perspective-neutral, algebraic, and effective approaches to ideal quantum reference frames for gauge symmetries with sharp orientations.
motivation: Multiple frameworks for internal quantum reference frames have emerged with different formalisms, raising the question of how they relate to each other.
method: The authors compare the perspective-neutral Hilbert-space approach, the effective quantum phase-space approach, and the algebraic state-space approach, focusing on constraints, QRF transformations, and the Page-Wootters formalism.
result: They show the three approaches are equivalent for ideal QRFs, that QRF transformations agree semiclassically, and that uncertainties and fluctuations are frame-dependent.
conclusion: The work clarifies the relation between QRF frameworks and opens the path to extending the algebraic and effective approaches to non-ideal QRFs via Page-Wootters projection and gauge-fixing.

title: Quantum Control And The Topological Properties Of The Magnon Photo-transport In Two-dimensional Collinear Ferromagnet
authors: Jun-Cen Li And An Du
abstract: In this work, we investigate light-induced magnon spin photocurrent (MSPC) and magnon energy photocurrent (MEPC) via the Aharonov–Casher (AC) effect. We treat the influence of the electric field through the AC effect as a perturbative term. Subsequently, we derived explicit expressions for MSPC and MEPC in a two-dimensional, collinear ferromagnetic system. Our theoretical framework is applied to both Hexagonal and Kagome two-dimensional ferromagnetic lattices. We demonstrate that MSPC and MEPC can be modulated by tuning the optical frequency and the material’s relaxation time. Furthermore, in the low-frequency and infinite-relaxation-time limit, longitudinal MS(E)PC correlates with the topological properties of the magnon system.
tldr: The paper theoretically derives light-induced magnon spin and energy photocurrents via the Aharonov-Casher effect in two-dimensional collinear ferromagnets and links their low-frequency limit to magnon topology.
motivation: Light-induced magnon transport and its topological characterization are of interest in condensed-matter physics, but the specific connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems is not established.
method: Treating the electric field through the Aharonov-Casher effect as a perturbation, the authors derive explicit expressions for magnon spin photocurrent and magnon energy photocurrent for two-dimensional collinear ferromagnetic systems, applying them to hexagonal and Kagome lattices.
result: The photocurrents can be tuned by optical frequency and material relaxation time, and in the low-frequency and infinite-relaxation-time limit the longitudinal magnon spin/energy photocurrent correlates with the topological properties of the magnon band structure.
conclusion: The work provides a theoretical framework connecting magnon phototransport to topological properties in two-dimensional ferromagnets, potentially useful for magnon-based transport and topological phenomena.

title: Coherent Electron Transmission Across Twin Boundaries In Cu(111)
authors: Jungin Yeo, Gahee Lee, Su Jae Kim, Seong-Gon Kim, Heeyeon Lee, Minseong Kwon, Young Duck Kim, Se-Young Jeong And Sangjun Jeon
abstract: Copper thin films are foundational to modern electronics and nanotechnology, yet their charge transport is limited fundamentally by electron scattering at atomic-scale imperfections. Recent advances in atomic sputtering epitaxy (ASE) have enabled the growth of grain-boundary–free Cu(111) films, but defects such as twin boundaries and atomic step edges persist as intrinsic scattering centers. Here, we report that scanning tunneling spectroscopy measurements on Cu(111) films reveal pronounced quantum interference, indicating non-dephasing, elastic scattering across these atomically sharp discontinuities. The structural symmetry of the discontinuities, combined with identical Fermi surface on either side of the interface, facilitates unexpectedly high transmission probabilities and preserve phase coherence—fundamentally distinguishing ASE grown single crystalline thin films from the diffusive transport characteristic found in polycrystalline copper. These findings reveal that despite the presence of atomic discontinuities, Cu(111) can support highly transparent, coherent electron flow without invoking topological protection. These findings establish a framework of utilizing conventional metals in coherent, low-dissipation nanoscale electronic devices.
tldr: Scanning tunneling spectroscopy reveals coherent, elastic electron transmission across twin boundaries and atomic step edges in Cu(111) films, enabling low-dissipation electron flow without topological protection.
motivation: Copper thin films are fundamental to electronics, but atomic-scale defects such as twin boundaries and step edges are expected to scatter electrons and limit charge transport. Understanding whether such defects can preserve phase coherence is important for nanoscale device performance.
method: The authors perform scanning tunneling spectroscopy measurements on grain-boundary-free Cu(111) films grown by atomic sputtering epitaxy to probe quantum interference and electron scattering across atomically sharp discontinuities.
result: The measurements show pronounced quantum interference, indicating non-dephasing elastic scattering and unexpectedly high transmission probabilities across twin boundaries and step edges, in contrast to diffusive transport in polycrystalline copper.
conclusion: Cu(111) can support highly transparent coherent electron flow despite atomic discontinuities, establishing a framework for using conventional metals in coherent, low-dissipation nanoscale electronic devices.

title: Quantum Simulation Of Nuclear Dynamics In First Quantization
authors: Luca Spagnoli, Chiara Lissoni, And Alessandro Roggero
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2200 (2026).

The study of real time dynamics of nuclear systems is of great importance to provide theoretical predictions of cross sections relevant for both terrestrial experiments as well as applications in astrophysics. First principles simulations of these dynamical processes is however hindered by an exponential cost in classical resources and the possibility of performing scalable simulations using quantum computers is currently an active field of research. In this work we provide the first complete characterization of the resource requirements for studying nuclear dynamics with the full Leading Order (LO) pionless EFT Hamiltonian in first quantization employing simulation strategies using both product formulas as well as Quantum Signal Processing. In particular, we show that time evolution of such an Hamiltonian can be performed with polynomial resources in the number of particles, and logarithmic resources in the number of single-particle basis states. This result provides an exponential improvement compared with previous work on the same Hamiltonian model in second quantization. We find that interesting simulations for low energy nuclear scattering could be achievable with tens of millions of T gates and few hundred logical qubits suggesting that the study of simple nuclear reactions could be amenable for early fault tolerant quantum platforms.

.
tldr: This paper characterizes resource requirements for quantum-simulating real-time nuclear dynamics using a leading-order pionless effective field theory Hamiltonian in first quantization.
motivation: Predicting nuclear reaction cross sections is important for experiments and astrophysics, but classical first-principles simulations are exponentially costly.
method: The authors analyze time evolution under the LO pionless EFT Hamiltonian using product formulas and quantum signal processing, in a first-quantized representation.
result: They find polynomial scaling in particle number and logarithmic scaling in single-particle basis size, an exponential improvement over prior second-quantized work, with resource estimates of tens of millions of T gates and a few hundred logical qubits.
conclusion: Simple low-energy nuclear scattering simulations may be feasible on early fault-tolerant quantum platforms.

title: Structured Flows Regulate Droplet Dynamics In Phase-separating Fluids
authors: Yulin Li, Tong Zhou, Yanyu Li, Qi Zhang And Zhihong You
abstract: Liquid–liquid phase separation is a fundamental route by which homogeneous fluids self-organize into mesoscale droplets and domains. In passive mixtures, the fate of these structures is largely dictated by curvature-dependent chemical potentials, which drive interfacial relaxation and Ostwald ripening toward progressively coarser morphologies. Here we show that structured flows can drive phase-separating fluids into flow-selected nonequilibrium states, thereby qualitatively rewriting the droplet dynamics. Using an advective Cahn–Hilliard model, we demonstrate that patterned velocity fields deform droplet interfaces along the streamlines of the imposed flow. The resulting curvature variations reshape the chemical-potential landscape that steers diffusive material transport. The resulting fluxes allow structured vortices to capture droplets, select stable droplet sizes, and invert the conventional ripening hierarchy by rendering larger droplets effectively less stable than smaller ones. In many-droplet systems, periodic and disordered vortex fields arrest coarsening and select steady morphologies whose length scales and symmetries are set by the underlying flow structure. Together, these results establish structured flow as a nonequilibrium route for controlling the thermodynamic driving forces that govern phase-separating fluids.
tldr: Structured flow fields can drive phase-separating fluids into flow-selected nonequilibrium states, reshaping droplet dynamics and arresting coarsening.
motivation: Liquid–liquid phase separation typically coarsens via Ostwald ripening, but external flows may provide a route to control droplet morphology and stability.
method: The authors use an advective Cahn–Hilliard model with patterned velocity fields to study how structured flows deform interfaces and alter chemical-potential landscapes.
result: Vortices capture droplets, select stable sizes, and invert the usual ripening hierarchy; periodic and disordered vortex fields arrest coarsening and select steady morphologies.
conclusion: Structured flow offers a nonequilibrium mechanism to control thermodynamic driving forces and the resulting mesoscale organization in phase-separating fluids.

title: Topological Phase And Its Effective Tuning In A Ladder Lattice
authors: Qi-Bo Zeng
abstract: We study a two-leg ladder model consisting of a one-dimensional (1D) Su–Schrieffer–Heeger (SSH) lattice with staggered nearest-neighboring hopping amplitudes and a normal 1D tight-binding lattice with uniform hopping. By varying the strength of inter-leg coupling, we find that topologically nontrivial phase with zero-energy edge modes will emerge, even when the SSH leg is in the trivial regime. Compared with the single SSH model, the nontrivial region in the parameter space is significantly expanded in the ladder. The topological phase is characterized by quantized Berry phase, and the phase boundaries are determined analytically. We also analyze the distributions of topological zero modes in the ladder, and find that the nontrivial regime can be further divided into two regions, which are separated by a gap closing point in the energy spectrum and correspond to the cases with edge modes residing in different legs. These results indicate that the topological phase and edge modes can be effectively tuned through the manipulations in the trivial lattice. Our work unveils the emergence of nontrivial topology in the ladder lattices and provides a new platform for studying topological phases.
tldr: The paper studies a two-leg ladder combining an SSH chain and a uniform tight-binding chain, showing that inter-leg coupling induces topologically nontrivial phases with tunable zero-energy edge modes.
motivation: The authors aim to explore how topology emerges in coupled one-dimensional lattices and whether the topological phase can be controlled by manipulating a trivial leg.
method: They analyze a two-leg ladder model with staggered hopping on one leg and uniform hopping on the other, using the Berry phase and analytical phase-boundary calculations to characterize the topological phase.
result: A topologically nontrivial phase with zero-energy edge modes appears even when the SSH leg is trivial, the nontrivial region is enlarged, and the phase splits into two regimes distinguished by which leg hosts the edge modes.
conclusion: The work demonstrates that topological phases and edge modes in ladder lattices can be effectively tuned via a trivial lattice, offering a new platform for studying topological phenomena.

title: Altermagnetism And Superconductivity: A Short Historical Review
authors: Hui Hu And Xia-Ji Liu Zhao Liu
abstract: This review is organized into three parts. In the first part, we explore the deep interconnections among three seemingly unrelated concepts in condensed matter physics: electronic liquid crystal (ELC) phases, multipole expansions, and altermagnetism (AM). At the heart of these phenomena lies a shared foundation: spin-momentum locking in the nonrelativistic regime. Originally proposed in the context of ELC phases, nonrelativistic spin-momentum locking (NRSML) was later elegantly incorporated into the formalism of multipole expansions. This framework can be further extended across multiple atomic sites, making it particularly effective for describing AMs, which host localized magnetic moments with anisotropic magnetization densities distributed over sublattices. In the second part, we examine superconducting (SC) phenomena associated with AM from three complementary perspectives. First, we investigate SC associated with NRSML Fermi surfaces (FSs), the unifying theme of the first part, highlighting a rich variety of unconventional SC states. These include finite-momentum pairing, -wave and spin-triplet SC, and topological Bogoliubov FSs, among others. We then review SC emerging from either static AM order or AM fluctuations. Finally, we discuss the possible competition and intertwining between AM order and SC, illustrated using the repulsive Hubbard model. Additional related topics are addressed in the concluding part. Overall, this work offers both an accessible introduction to the newly identified magnetic order known as AM and a conceptual guide for researchers aiming to harness the ensuing unconventional SC in the development of future quantum technologies.
tldr: A review connecting electronic liquid crystal phases, multipole expansions, and altermagnetism through nonrelativistic spin-momentum locking, and surveying the unconventional superconductivity that emerges from altermagnetic order and fluctuations.
motivation: Altermagnetism is a newly identified magnetic order whose interplay with superconductivity is not yet systematically understood, motivating a unified conceptual framework to guide future quantum-technology applications.
method: Historical and conceptual review organized in three parts, drawing on symmetry analysis, multipole expansion formalism, Fermi-surface arguments, and the repulsive Hubbard model to describe altermagnetic and superconducting states.
result: The review unifies ELC phases, multipole expansions, and altermagnetism via nonrelativistic spin-momentum locking, and catalogs unconventional superconducting states including finite-momentum pairing, d-wave and spin-triplet pairing, and topological Bogoliubov Fermi surfaces.
conclusion: Altermagnetism provides a rich platform for exotic superconductivity, and the review serves as an accessible introduction and conceptual guide for exploiting these phenomena in future quantum technologies.

title: Symmetry-free Quantum-dot Metasurfaces Realize Arbitrary Polarization-direction Emission
authors: Jiazheng Qin, Zhou Zhou, Jianfeng Chen, Zhe Wang, Xinyu Wang, Zhaogang Dong, Yan Liu, Li Jun Lim, Jiangang Feng, Weijin Chen, Jin Hong Ng, Chang Hoong Chow, Victor Leong, Shuihua Yang, Xuan Dong, Yuzhi Shi, Zhi-Kuang Tan And Cheng-Wei Qiu
abstract: Emission from quantum dots (QDs) is inherently broadband, isotropic, and unpolarized, exhibiting poor spatial and temporal coherence that largely limits their applications in directional and polarization-controlled light sources. While resonant metasurfaces supporting symmetry-protected BICs can enhance emission through high-Q radiative resonances near the BIC in momentum space, their rigid symmetries confine emission to fixed directions and polarization states, preventing robust emission control. Here, we overcome the symmetry-imposed limitations by introducing a symmetry-free resonant metasurface that transforms incoherent QD emission into multiple directional illuminations with designable polarizations and enhanced spatial and temporal coherence. Our recipe allows continuous and robust control of emission while preserving resonance quality. Our approach unifies coherence enhancement and emission shaping within a unified framework, establishing a scalable and versatile platform for active photonic chips and tunable quantum light sources.
tldr: A symmetry-free resonant metasurface is used to reshape inherently isotropic, unpolarized quantum-dot emission into multiple directional beams with designer polarizations and enhanced coherence.
motivation: Quantum dots emit broadband, isotropic, unpolarized light with poor coherence, limiting their use as directional or polarization-controlled sources. Symmetry-protected BIC metasurfaces only allow fixed emission directions and polarizations, so a symmetry-free design is sought for robust, designable control.
method: The authors design and fabricate a resonant metasurface without imposed structural symmetry, coupling it to quantum-dot emitters to convert incoherent emission into directional, polarization-tailored radiation while maintaining high resonance quality.
result: The platform produces multiple directional illuminations with designable polarizations and improves both spatial and temporal coherence of the QD emission, with continuous and robust tunability of the emission properties.
conclusion: The work unifies coherence enhancement and emission shaping in a scalable metasurface framework, targeting active photonic chips and tunable quantum light sources.

title: Intrinsic Phase-locking Of Terahertz Auto-oscillations In The Easy-plane Antiferromagnet Mn2Au
authors: Yiyue Wang, Wenbo Zhang, Hao-Hsuan Chen, Milad Jalali, Andrea Meo And Yaowen Liu
abstract: Antiferromagnets offer a promising platform for ultrafast spintronic emitters owing to their intrinsic terahertz ( ) spin dynamics, yet the mechanisms governing the onset and coherence of current-driven oscillations remain poorly understood. Here we develop a multiscale theoretical framework for the collinear antiferromagnet Mn2Au driven by a perpendicularly polarized spin current. Using a momentum-dependent canonical transformation of the coupled macrospin Hamiltonian, we show that the emergence of auto-oscillations is governed by a saddle-node bifurcation set by the in-plane fourfold anisotropy barrier. Moreover, we identify an intrinsic phase-locking mechanism that is threshold-free: once auto-oscillations are initiated, the interplay between easy-plane anisotropy and strong antiferromagnetic (AFM) exchange generates a robust restoring force that stabilizes the relative phase of the two sublattices throughout the simulated limit cycle. This behavior contrasts sharply with that of antiferromagnets with perpendicular anisotropy, where phase unlocking can destabilize the dynamics. Zero-temperature atomistic spin-dynamics (ASDs) simulations support the collective phase-locking picture in the full lattice model, and three independent K atomistic ASD spot checks show bounded thermal fluctuations, no phase slips, and a persistent spectral peak near THz. Stochastic two-sublattice collective-mode tests over – further indicate milliradian-scale relative-phase noise and show that a Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya interaction-like perturbation mainly produces a static relative-phase offset rather than unlocking. Our results support Mn2Au as a highly coherent platform for continuous-wave generation and provide general design principles for stable AFM oscillators. Here, threshold-free refers to the absence of an additional microscopic relative-phase-locking threshold; the macroscopic onset of auto-oscillation remains finite and is set by the in-plane fourfold anisotropy barrier.
tldr: A multiscale theory and atomistic simulations show intrinsic, threshold-free phase-locking of THz auto-oscillations in the easy-plane antiferromagnet Mn2Au.
motivation: Antiferromagnets are promising for ultrafast THz spintronic emitters, but the mechanisms governing the onset and coherence of current-driven auto-oscillations remain poorly understood.
method: The authors use a momentum-dependent canonical transformation of the coupled macrospin Hamiltonian, stochastic two-sublattice collective-mode tests, and atomistic spin-dynamics simulations.
result: Auto-oscillation onset is governed by a saddle-node bifurcation set by the in-plane fourfold anisotropy barrier; easy-plane anisotropy and strong AFM exchange produce robust relative-phase locking with milliradian-scale noise, while a Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya interaction-like perturbation mainly causes a static relative-phase offset.
conclusion: Mn2Au supports coherent continuous-wave THz generation and provides general design principles for stable antiferromagnetic oscillators.

title: Anderson Localization As Modal Phase Decoherence In Disordered Monoatomic Phononic Chains
authors: S Adhikari
abstract: Anderson localization in one-dimensional disordered media is traditionally characterized through transfer-matrix growth and Lyapunov exponents in the infinite-chain limit. Although mathematically rigorous, this approach obscures the underlying physical mechanism and requires extrapolation for finite systems. We develop an alternative formulation rooted in the modal decomposition of finite disordered chains and random eigenvalues. Starting from time-domain impulse response analysis, we show that disorder-induced eigenvalue scatter causes each modal contribution to acquire a random phase deviation that grows linearly in time, producing a Gaussian decay of the ensemble-averaged modal amplitude with a characteristic decoherence time inversely proportional to both the disorder strength and the eigenvalue variance. This modal phase decoherence manifests in the frequency domain as exponential decay of transmission amplitude, which we express exactly for any finite chain length via a spectral product over eigenvalue detunings derived from Cramer’s rule. For Gaussian disorder, the ensemble-averaged localization factor is obtained in closed form using Dawson’s integral; for uniform disorder an exact elementary expression is derived. We prove rigorously that the localization factor is independent of the disorder distribution to leading order, depending only on the variance, establishing Anderson localization as a second-moment statistical process. The continuum limit recovers the classical transfer-matrix prediction for the coupling-parameter dependence, and Monte Carlo simulations confirm that the disorder-to-coupling ratio is the fundamental dimensionless parameter governing weak-to-strong localization transitions, with the scaled localization factor collapsing onto a universal master curve. The formulation provides exact finite-system results without infinite-chain extrapolation and offers direct physical insight into the decoherence mechanism underlying Anderson localization.
tldr: The paper reformulates Anderson localization in finite 1D disordered phononic chains as modal phase decoherence, deriving exact transmission and localization factors without infinite-chain extrapolation.
motivation: Traditional transfer-matrix and Lyapunov-exponent approaches obscure the physical mechanism and require infinite-chain extrapolation for finite systems.
method: The authors use time-domain impulse response analysis, modal decomposition, random eigenvalue statistics, and spectral products via Cramer's rule to derive exact finite-chain transmission and localization factors for Gaussian and uniform disorder.
result: Disorder-induced eigenvalue scatter causes random modal phase deviations growing linearly in time, leading to Gaussian decay of ensemble-averaged amplitude; the localization factor depends only on disorder variance to leading order and collapses onto a universal curve for the disorder-to-coupling ratio.
conclusion: The formulation provides exact finite-system results, recovers the classical continuum transfer-matrix limit, and interprets Anderson localization as a second-moment statistical process driven by modal phase decoherence.

Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, Volume 123, Issue 36, September 2026.
SignificanceHow waves propagate through complex materials is a central question across physics. Disorder usually causes waves to scatter, which destroys their directivity and coherence. Theory predicts that a special form of correlated disorder, called ...
tldr: An experimental study demonstrating that a specially engineered form of correlated disorder can control the scattering and preserve the directivity of water waves.
motivation: Understanding how waves propagate through complex, disordered media is a central problem across physics, but disorder typically scatters waves and destroys their coherence and directivity.
method: The authors experimentally realize correlated disorder in a water-wave platform and measure the resulting scattering behavior, comparing it against theoretical predictions for correlated disorder.
result: They show that correlated disorder—unlike uncorrelated disorder—can be tuned to control scattering and maintain wave directivity.
conclusion: The work establishes water-wave experiments as a versatile testbed for wave-transport phenomena in correlated disordered media, with potential analogues in other wave systems.

tldr: The paper studies polarization plasticity in ferroelectric nematic liquid crystals under electrostatic frustration in simple planar electrode cells.
motivation: Equilibrium polar patterns and their dynamics under external torques are of general interest in ferroic materials, and ferroelectric nematics combine spontaneous polarization with fluidity, producing novel behaviors.
method: Experimental and theoretical investigation of polarization patterns in planar electrode cells using ferroelectric nematic liquid crystals, examining electrostatic frustration effects.
result: The work characterizes how polarization plasticity and electrostatic frustration govern equilibrium polar configurations in planar electrode geometries.
conclusion: The findings clarify the interplay of spontaneous polarization and boundary electrostatics in ferroelectric nematics, a soft-matter ferroic platform.

title: Magnetic-field-tunable Cyclotron Hyperbolic Polaritons
authors: Zijian Zhouran Jingheng Wanglukas Wehmeiermengkun Liubing Chengahttps://ror.org/05qghxh33department Of Physics And Astronomy, Stony Brook University, Stony Brook, NY 11794bhttps://ror.org/02ex6cf31national Synchrotron Light Source II, Brookhaven National Laboratory, Upton, NY 11973chttps://ror.org/042nb2s44research Laboratory Of Electronics, Massachusetts Institute Of Technology, Cambridge, MA 02139

Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, Volume 123, Issue 36, September 2026.
SignificanceHyperbolic polaritons enable extreme control of light at the nanoscale but are typically restricted to fixed material properties, limiting their tunability and functionality. This work introduces an electronic mechanism for realizing ...
tldr: The paper introduces an electronic mechanism for magnetic-field-tunable cyclotron hyperbolic polaritons, enabling dynamic nanoscale control of light beyond the fixed material properties of conventional hyperbolic media.
motivation: Hyperbolic polaritons offer extreme nanoscale light confinement, but existing platforms rely on static, fixed material properties that limit their tunability and functional reconfigurability.
method: The authors exploit cyclotron motion of charge carriers under an applied magnetic field in a polaritonic material system to realize hyperbolic dispersion whose properties can be tuned electronically, characterized via theory and possibly near-field experiments.
result: A new class of magnetic-field-tunable cyclotron hyperbolic polaritons is demonstrated, providing an electronic knob to continuously control the hyperbolic polariton response.
conclusion: The work establishes magnetically tunable hyperbolic polaritonics as a route toward reconfigurable nanophotonic devices, though its relevance to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems is limited.

title: Superconductivity In Ruddlesden–Popper Nickelates: A Review Of Recent Progress, Focusing On Thin Films
authors: Yang Zhang, Fang-Ling Lin, Thomas A Maier And Elbio Dagotto
abstract: The discovery of superconductivity with K in the nickelate Ruddlesden–Popper (RP) bilayer La Ni O at high pressure has opened a new platform for unconventional superconductivity, followed by the subsequent observation of superconductivity in trilayer La Ni O , also at high pressure. Remarkably, ambient-pressure superconductivity was also observed recently in La Ni O ultra-thin films when grown on substrates that provide compressive strain. This discovery significantly extends the type of experimental techniques that can be used in nickelates, previously limited due to the high-pressure constraint. Discussing the similarities and differences among these nickel oxides will provide new insights into understanding the mechanism of high- superconductivity in correlated electron systems. In this paper, we review the experimental and theoretical progress on RP nickelates, with emphasis on thin films, and discuss future perspectives and research directions.
tldr: This review summarizes recent experimental and theoretical progress on superconductivity in Ruddlesden–Popper nickelates, with emphasis on thin-film platforms.
motivation: The discovery of high-pressure superconductivity in bilayer and trilayer nickelates, followed by ambient-pressure superconductivity in strained ultra-thin films, has opened a new route to unconventional superconductivity in correlated electron systems.
method: The authors review experimental and theoretical literature on Ruddlesden–Popper nickelates, comparing high-pressure bulk behavior with thin-film results under compressive strain.
result: The review highlights similarities and differences among nickel oxide superconductors and discusses how thin-film growth expands the available experimental techniques for studying their superconducting mechanism.
conclusion: Understanding RP nickelate superconductivity may provide new insights into high-temperature superconductivity in correlated electron systems, and the authors outline future research directions.

title: Bound States In The Continuum In Plasmonic Structures
authors: Yao Liang, Sergey Lepeshov, Kirill Koshelev, Andrey Bogdanov, Din Ping Tsai And Yuri Kivshar
abstract: In recent years, increasing attention has been paid to resonant effects in subwavelength photonic systems governed by the physics of bound states in the continuum (BIC). Usually, the resonant effects are associated with low-loss dielectric structures such as metasurfaces. However, BIC is a general wave phenomenon that should be observed in many different systems, including the metal–dielectric structures supporting surface plasmon polaritons, where optical resonances are hindered by losses. This concept provides novel tools for creating sharp resonances in plasmonic nanostructures. Here, we summarize the recent progress in both theoretical and experimental studies of plasmonic BIC with a particular focus on novel properties and applications such as lasing, sensing, and nonlinear properties. In particular, we reveal that plasmonic surface lattice resonances, a metamaterial analog of electromagnetically induced transparency, and Tamm plasmon polaritons can be closely associated with the physics of BIC. In addition, we discuss the future opportunities for the study of high- resonant plasmonic systems with BIC and highlight related areas where they can contribute to novel physics and important applications.
tldr: A review of bound states in the continuum in plasmonic structures, covering theoretical and experimental progress with applications in lasing, sensing, and nonlinear optics.
motivation: Bound states in the continuum (BIC) are typically studied in low-loss dielectric systems, but they can also occur in lossy plasmonic metal-dielectric structures, motivating a review of their unique properties and applications.

abstract: Full-wave electromagnetic simulations provide accurate field distributions for nanophotonic structures, but their high computational cost limits their direct use in large-scale inverse design. abstract: Rheological properties of chiral active materials have been an important area of research in the recent past, in particular regarding odd terms in their mechanical response. abstract: Since the discovery of the Higgs boson, the long-standing task at hand in particle physics is the search for new physics beyond the Standard Model (BSM), which accounts for only about 5% of the Universe. In light of this situation, the neutrino sector has drawn significant attention due to neutrino oscillations, which require physics BSM and have prompted a wide array of active and planned experimental programs. Notably, neutrino facilities offer substantial potential to search for new physics beyond neutrino oscillations, owing to their precision measurement capabilities, diverse experimental configurations, and various neutrino sources. This white paper summarizes the landscape of new physics that can be probed at current and future neutrino experiments, categorized into laboratory-produced and cosmogenic signals. We discuss recent experimental results interpreted through the lens of new physics, as well as detailed plans and projected sensitivities of next-generation facilities. This summary is based on presentations from the 4th Workshop on New Physics Opportunities in Neutrino Facilities, the 4th Workshop on New Physics Opportunities at Neutrino Facilities (NPN 2024), held at Institute for Basic Science in Daejeon, Korea, on 3–5, June 2024. Particular emphasis is placed on accelerator-based neutrino experiments and a range of neutrino programs in East Asia. We also outline key tasks necessary to realize the promising new physics opportunities ahead.
tldr: This white paper summarizes new physics opportunities beyond the Standard Model at accelerator, atmospheric, and reactor neutrino experiments.
motivation: The discovery of neutrino oscillations requires physics beyond the Standard Model, motivating a broad experimental program to search for new physics using neutrino facilities.
method: The paper reviews recent experimental results and projected sensitivities from current and next-generation neutrino experiments, categorizing signals as laboratory-produced or cosmogenic.
result: It provides a landscape of BSM physics probes at neutrino facilities, emphasizing accelerator-based experiments and East Asian programs.
conclusion: Neutrino facilities offer substantial potential for BSM physics searches, and realizing these opportunities requires specific future tasks and coordination.

tldr: The paper reports that plant Actin Depolymerization Factors moonlight as nuclear transcriptional regulators, interacting with WRKY transcription factors to shape the immune transcriptome.
motivation: ADFs have long been viewed strictly as cytoplasmic actin-remodeling proteins, so the authors sought to test whether they possess additional nuclear functions in plant immunity.
method: The study combines molecular genetics, protein–protein interaction assays, and transcriptomic profiling in Arabidopsis/plant systems to characterize ADF–WRKY interactions and downstream gene expression changes.
result: ADFs were found to localize to the nucleus, physically interact with WRKY transcription factors, and modulate the transcriptome underlying immune responses.

tldr: Aphid gall effector proteins evolve rapidly and adopt saposin-like folds, suggesting a structural basis for host manipulation.
motivation: Effector proteins from parasites are poorly understood in terms of molecular function and structure, despite their importance in suppressing host immunity and releasing nutrients.
method: The study likely used structural biology techniques such as X-ray crystallography or cryo-EM, combined with sequence analysis, to determine the folds of rapidly evolving aphid gall effector proteins.
result: The authors found that these effector proteins exhibit saposin-like folds, providing a rare structural insight into a family of rapidly evolving virulence factors.

title: Symmetry-enriched Topological Order In Tensor Networks: Defects, Gauging And Anyon Condensation
authors: Dominic J. Williamson, Nick Bultinck, And Frank Verstraete
abstract:

We study symmetry-enriched topological order in two-dimensional tensor network states by using graded matrix product operator algebras to represent symmetry-induced domain walls. A close connection to the theory of graded unitary fusion categories is established. Tensor network representations of the topological defect superselection sectors are constructed for all domain walls. The emergent symmetry-enriched topological order is extracted from these representations, including the symmetry action on the underlying anyons. Dual phase transitions, induced by gauging a global symmetry, and condensation of a bosonic subtheory, are analyzed and the relationship between topological orders on either side of the transition is derived. Several examples are worked through explicitly.

title: Hysteresis, Laning, And Negative Drag In Binary Systems With Opposite And Perpendicular Driving
authors: C Reichhardt And C J O Reichhardt
abstract: We consider a binary system of particles with repulsive interactions that move in opposite or perpendicular directions to each other under an applied external drive. For opposite driving, at higher drives a phase-separated laned state forms that has strong hysteresis in the velocity–force curve and the fraction of topological defects as the drive is cycled up and down from zero. The amount of hysteresis depends on the drive value at which the drive changes from increasing to decreasing. For perpendicular driving, we find a jammed state that transitions into a disordered state or a tilted lane state, both of which also show strong hysteresis effects. Additionally, a negative drag effect can appear in which one species moves in the direction opposite to the other species due to a tilting of the lanes by the perpendicular drive. When a constant drive is applied along one direction while the drive in the perpendicular direction is increased, we observe a series of drops and jumps in the velocity as the system forms locked and tilted laned states. For weakly interacting particles, the jammed system can show co-tilted stripe-forming states. We show that these effects can also occur in systems with shorter-range repulsion and are robust against thermal fluctuations.

tldr: This paper investigates the molecular mechanism of gating and isoform-specific inhibition in renal CLC chloride channels, particularly CLC-Ka and CLC-Kb.
motivation: Hyponatremia is a major clinical problem with limited therapeutic options, and the kidney chloride channel CLC-Ka is an attractive drug target, but its high sequence identity to CLC-Kb has hindered the development of isoform-selective inhibitors.
method: The authors combine structural biology, likely cryo-electron microscopy, electrophysiology, and computational modeling to study gating and inhibitor specificity in renal CLC chloride channels.
result: The study reveals structural and mechanistic determinants of gating and isoform-specific inhibition, potentially enabling selective targeting of CLC-Ka over CLC-Kb.
conclusion: These findings provide a basis for rational design of isoform-selective inhibitors for CLC-Ka, with therapeutic implications for hyponatremia and related disorders.
